Mr. Chairman, when the committee was adjourned at five o'clock I was discussing the need for federal legislation which would give the federal government
Criminal Code
power to deal with the pollution of interprovincial rivers. On January 19, the hon. member for Prince Albert asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare a question. The minister replied as follows as reported at page 1234 of Hansard:
My hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of his question. He asks first of all what, pursuant to the inquiry made of my officers in my absence, was the situation resulting from communications made by the Department of National Health and Welfare to the appropriate departments of health of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Contact has been made with the officers in the two departments of the two provinces. The facts of the matter have been ascertained.
This is what I want the committee to note.
The responsibility for remedying the situation is recognized by both provinces as not coming within the competence of the federal government. Indeed, whether or not there was that acknowledgment I would have to submit that would have to be the situation as far as the federal government is concerned, for this is clearly a matter that does not come within the competence of the federal government.
As I emphasized in my remarks before the recess, the people in my constituency who are affected by this pollution have urged me to get this government to introduce legislation which would give them some protection. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said that the province of Alberta had the authority to deal with this matter and was fully capable of dealing with it. I wish to put section 12, chapter 53 of the Alberta public health act on record. The act states:
The provincial board shall have the general supervision of all springs, wells, ponds, lakes, streams or rivers used as a source of a public water supply, or for agricultural, domestic or industrial purposes with reference to their purity, together with the waters feeding the same, and shall examine the same from time to time when the necessity for such examination arises, and inquire what, if any, pollution exists and the causes thereof.
They only have to examine the water when the necessity for examination arises and inquire what, if any, pollution exists and the causes thereof. The act continues:
The provincial board may inquire into and hear and determine any complaint made by or on behalf of a riparian proprietor entitled to the use of water, that any industrial waste or any other polluting material of any kind whatsoever, which either by itself or in connection with other matter may corrupt or impair the quality of the water or may render such water unfit for accustomed or ordinary use, has been placed in or discharged into such water, or placed or deposited upon the ice thereof, or placed or suffered to remain upon the bank or shore thereof. The provincial board may make a report to the minister upon such complaint and as to what remedial measures, if any, are required in respect to any alleged injury or invasion of right as it may deem just.
Where the report of the provincial board recommends the removal or degree of treatment of any such polluting material, any riparian proprietor interested or the minister may apply to a judge of the supreme court or to a district court judge

Criminal Code
by way of originating notice according to the practice of the court, for an order for the removal or abatement of the injury in terms of the report of the provincial board and to restrain the proprietors of the industry from carrying on the same, or the proprietors or other offending party or parties from continuing the acts complained of until the injury or invasion of right has been abated to the satisfaction of the provincial board.
That is quite all right as far as it goes, but there is no penalty provided in the act after what I might call the crime has been committed. When the board issued an order to the Canadian Chemical Company to stop pouring certain elements into the river the company did what they could. They put up a temporary pipe and that pipe was used to divert certain elements for 24 hours, but after 24 hours the pipe was clogged with residue. What did they do? Did they shut the plant down? No, they turned it right back into the river again. I for one cannot understand why this company which knew of the distress which was being caused to 25,000 or 30,000 people did not close their plant down until they could erect a permanent take-off or pipeline. But instead of that they put the stuff back into the river and it was allowed to run into the river for another 36 hours.
The Prince Albert city council held a meeting a report of which is contained in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 16. Here is the report in part:
Our solicitors tell us that company officials worked frantically to clear the obstruction in the pipes last week. But they were not frantic enough to close the plant.
That is the Canadian Chemical Company.
I note, too, that a director of the plant, a Col. H. A. Eydt, expressed annoyance at the publicity given the re-pollution of the river.
I said earlier that the people in my constituency wanted this mess cleaned up. The hon. member for Prince Albert in his remarks stated he had never seen the people in that part of the country so worked up over anything as they are over this particular situation. I am not going to read the dozens of letters I have received, but I want to put two or three editorials on the record. These are newspaper editorials and have no particular political background. I have one here, the North Battleford News-Optimist. I am not going to read it all, but 1 will read the last part:
Whatever the truth may be one thing is certain.
And here I would like to make a correction. The minister has mentioned North Battleford in connection with pollution several times, but the city of North Battleford is not affected. The city of North Battleford is using well water. But the town of Battleford is affected. The editorial continues:
North Battleford is blessed with untainted water. What a blessing that is!

At Battleford, the Saskatchewan hospital, Prince Albert, and numerous other communities up and down the North Saskatchewan river, a real threat exists. The water smells ... it tastes like varnish.
That any single industry should so pollute a nation's natural resource is a crime that should be punishable by the law of the land. We in North Battleford who fortunately have not suffered should, and we sure do support our brothers in their fight to have this menace dealt with by the government at Ottawa.
And then the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix had this to say:
It is true, no doubt, that the water pollution from which North Battleford and Prince Albert-
They are wrong again there. They say "North Battleford". It should be Battleford.
-are now suffering does not make the North Saskatchewan river any less navigable than usual. From this point of view, Mr. Chevrier's objection to Mr. Campbell's proposal to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act to take account of the difficulty may have been justified. But the Minister of Transport did not argue on that basis alone. He seemed to be claiming that it would be unconstitutional for parliament to legislate at all with respect to a form of pollution which does not affect navigation or fisheries and may not be medically injurious to health.
We should like to see Mr. Chevrier's opinion tested in the courts, especially if investigation proves the theory that the pollution originates in Alberta.
And that theory has been proven.
For whatever the health implications, there is no doubt, we think, that the taste and smell of their domestic water are more than annoyances to the people of the two Saskatchewan cities. People just will not drink disagreeable water if they can help it; and because they will not North Battleford, Prince Albert and perhaos other communities along the river may suffer economically.
Then I have another editorial again from the North Battleford News-Optimist which reads as follows:
We sympathize with the residents of Battleford. Their water tastes like varnish and smells like . . ., well, it smells like varnish too. Some 3,400 residents of Battleford and the Saskatchewan hospital are presently suffering from the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river.
Fortunately, the people of the city of North Battleford are not affected. They derive their water from wells which have not yet been tainted.
It is unfortunate that governments act so slow. The government of Saskatchewan has not been able to deal effectively with the government of Alberta. It thus seems time that the senior government at Ottawa should step into the picture immediately and settle this issue. The pollution cannot be allowed to continue, for not only is it obnoxious to the taste and smell, but there is a new fear growing among members of the medical profession at Prince Albert that it is also injurious to our people's health.
The water of the great rivers belongs to all the people of Canada. We cannot afford at any time to allow industries to destroy it. The waters of the North Saskatchewan river are a resource which must be protected since it would not be possible for the thousands of people who depend upon it for water to live without it comfortably.

Then Godfrey Hudson whom all of the western members will know-he is one of Canada's noted news commentators-has this to say in a commentary he made on February 24:
The water in the rivers of this country belongs to the Canadian people. Yet a member of the federal cabinet has said that industries and communities from coast to coast have been polluting river water for years, and that the federal government has no jurisdiction over pollution. We think it is high time the federal government amended the constitution, if necessary, to get the power to control the dumping of wastes into rivers. The federal government has the power to control navigation in our rivers. If it is important enough for Ottawa to wield control over navigation, surely it is important enough for Ottawa to exercise control over something that affects the well-being of tens of thousands of Canadians.
We submit that the awful water that the people of Battleford, the patients and the staff of the Saskatchewan hospital at North Battleford, the residents of Prince Albert and the residents of The Pas, Manitoba, have had to drink in recent months has shown a glaring weakness in the present division of powers between the provinces and the federal government. There should be federal legislation establishing uniform control coast to coast over what can be dumped into rivers that are sources of drinking water. And any industry or municipal corporation that plans to dump waste into a river should have to get a federal health permit before getting a construction permit.
That is just what I was saying before supper. Most of what has been said has had to do with humans but we have fisheries legislation in Canada. What has happened to the fish in the North Saskatchewan river? Here is an article from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 16, from the Prince Albert correspondent:
"The chemical pollution of the North Saskatchewan river threatens to wipe out the fish population of the river," A. H. McDonald, director of the fisheries branch of the Saskatchewan department of natural resources, stated here Monday afternoon. A full report on the situation is to be made to the provincial government and federal department of fisheries.
At the same time, city council here, through its Edmonton solicitors, said it would take legal action against the Canadian Chemical Company at Edmonton, unless concrete assurances were given that no more polluting chemicals would be placed in the river by the company.
Then I am passing over and leaving out a portion of this article which continues further on as follows:
In his fisheries report, Mr. McDonald said tests conducted by his department during the last month had shown a "dangerously low oxygen content" of the water of the river and that the chemicals present appeared to be responsible. "We have noted increasing numbers of dead fish in the river, with a total of 130 dead fish being noted at one small open area near the city."
He said the situation was better downstream, after the junction of the north and south branches of the Saskatchewan river. However, at Cumberland House the fish, while alive, were unfit to eat because of an offensively oily taste, and residents had discontinued fishing.

Recent tests conducted at Prince Albert, when fish from the South Saskatchewan were kept in observation tanks at the power house here, showed that fish placed in a wire screen under the ice, died within an hour of being placed in the water.
The oxygen content of the river necessary for proper fish respiration varies from five to nine parts per million parts of water, Mr. McDonald said. "As far west as Frenchman Butte, the average oxygen content of the North Saskatchewan river is approximately one part per million," he said. "In comparison, the water of the South Saskatchewan at St. Louis averages 13 parts per million, which is good for the time of the year."
"Our biologists are of the opinion that few fish can survive the condition prevalent in the North Saskatchewan," Mr. McDonald said.
What does that mean? That means that it is almost certain that there is not a live fish in the North Saskatchewan river today. How many fish are in the river normally? I do not know. There are probably hundreds of thousands. What is going to happen now when the river has perhaps hundreds of thousands of dead fish in it? How is it going to affect the health of our people? Our people write me and tell me that they are now desperately afraid of a typhoid epidemic. There is a great deal more that I could say, but I do not want to take up any more of the time of the committee. However, I want to make this plea to the government. Our people are looking to this government across the way to bring in legislation that will definitely put a stop to this sort of thing. They are looking, not only to me and to the hon. member for Prince Albert to make a fight but to the other members from the province of Saskatchewan and to every member of the house who may possibly find himself and his constituency in the same position.
It can happen to other constituencies besides Prince Albert and The Battlefords. I appeal, I plead with the government of Canada to take remedial action first of all to bring in health laws which will prevent any industry from commencing business until such time as it has given assurance that it is not going to pollute our rivers. In the second place, we want legislation in the Criminal Code which will make it a crime for any industry to do what the Canadian Chemical Company did. They set up a mechanical monster that can do even greater and bigger things than Paul Bunyan and his blue ox. In the early days on the western plains people used to tell great stories about Paul Bunyan and his blue ox, about what the blue ox could do and what Paul Bunyan could do, but this mechanical monster can put its odours and stenches into every home in the city of Prince Albert, the town of Battleford and even into the provincial hospital.
Surely it is time that we did something to stop this. I want to hear from the Minister

Criminal Code
of National Health and Welfare and I want to hear from the Minister of Justice and others. I suggested an amendment a couple of weeks ago. I do not want to try to amend the Criminal Code because I am not a lawyer. That is the job of the government across the way. That is the job that our people are looking to you to do. Let us hear what you will do about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with the great and rapid growth of the petrochemical and other types of industry in the oil fields of northern Alberta I think we can all agree that the nation is faced with the problem of what to do with the river pollution which could be caused by such industries in northern Alberta unless something is done to prevent it. Western Canada is faced for the first time with a problem that has been common in eastern Canada, namely, how, under the pressure of industrial development, the rivers of the country can be put to the most advantageous use. I do not think there will be any argument as to the necessity of our facing up to the problem. Perhaps the only argument that will develop is as to the best methods of solving it.
I should like to examine the matter tonight from that standpoint, and to begin with an examination of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert since that is the immediate question before us. Then, because I think that is not a satisfactory method, I should like to move on to suggest others which in my view would be much more satisfactory than the one he has suggested. First of all I should like to deal with some of the facts which he mentioned in his remarks. The first one is that he stated that the corporation in question had stopped the practice of discharging effluent into the river. As we will recall, on the last occasion on which we discussed this matter the problem was not quite that which we have tonight. The problem then was to find out what the facts were.
I suggested on that occasion that it would be impossible, no matter what clauses we had in the Criminal Code, to lay a charge against the guilty corporation until we knew what the facts were and knew which corporation was the guilty one. If my hon. friend will recall, I also suggested that I thought that when we found out what the facts were I would be very much surprised indeed if, when confronted with those facts, the corporation in question would not be quite willing to desist from the practice of discharging its effluent into the river without the necessity of any prosecution at all. It was very gratifying to have the hon. member for Prince Albert tell us this afternoon that

that is precisely what has happened, that when the facts were established and the company in question was confronted with them it did desist although, as the hon. member for The Battlefords suggested, there was a short period of time during which the arrangements it made to divert its effluent from the Saskatchewan river broke down.
The suggestion is now made that there is no offence in the code covering this act, and in due course I want to take issue with that statement. The hon. member for Prince Albert having alleged that there now is no offence covering the act of pollution suggests an amendment to provide such an offence. I should like to deal with his amendment. To begin with, I think the amendment is made to quite an inappropriate clause of the bill. It is made to section 163 which comes under the general heading of "Disturbing religious services". This section 163 in its present form is aimed at those who, as set out in the second subsection (b) of this section, throw a stink bomb or stench bomb or device from which any offensive volatile substance mentioned in paragraph (a) of the same section is or is capable of being liberated, and is likely to alarm, inconvenience, discommode or cause discomfort to any person or to cause damage to property.
I do not think that is an appropriate section to amend for the purpose of preventing the discharge of effluent into a river. But I am not stating that as a captious criticism because I will admit at once that if section 163 is not an appropriate section to amend it would be a very simple matter, once we had concluded that such an amendment was the proper method of dealing with the problem, to select a suitable section of the code or to create a new and suitable section to deal with this matter.

Right on that point I would point out to my hon. friend that the reference to disturbing religious services cannot apply to this group of sections in general because section 162 says:
Every one who, without lawful excuse, the proof of which lies upon him, loiters or prowls at night upon the property of another person near a dwelling house situated on that property is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
That has nothing to do with church services at all. As a matter of fact the heading for this group of sections is not a correct designation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at the section that he is seeking to amend, he will see that the significant words in it read as follows:
Every one other than a peace officer . . . who deposits, throws or injects or causes to be deposited, thrown or injected in, into or near any place,

(a)	an offensive volatile substance that is likely to alarm, inconvenience, discommode or cause discomfort to any person or to cause damage to property, or
(b)	a stink or stench bomb or device from which any substance mentioned in paragraph (a) is or is capable of being liberated . . .
It deals with stench bombs or the contents of stench bombs and their discharge in or near any place to the alarm, inconvenience or discomfort of the people there. As I say, I am not raising this as a captious criticism, because it is quite apparent that if we want to solve the problem of the use of the waters of the North Saskatchewan river by creating new crimes by an amendment to the criminal law-it is a very easy matter, if we do not adopt my hon. friend's amendment, to produce an amendment which would be more appropriate for that purpose.
But what I do suggest is this, that when my hon. friend says there is no offence in Bill No. 7 which covers this act, I would refer him to clause 165 which provides:
Every one who commits a common nuisance and thereby
(a)	endangers the lives, safety or health of the public, or
(b)	causes physical injury to any person
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
Now, the offence my hon. friend was proposing to create was an offence punishable upon summary conviction. It is true that when he moved his amendment he suggested it could be changed to be made punishable upon indictment. But until that change was made, the only penalty which could be imposed upon an accused corporation would be a fine of $1,000 which, I think, under the circumstances we have been considering, would not likely be an effective deterrent. The section dealing with a common nuisance, which I was reading, goes on to define a common nuisance in these terms:
For the purposes of this section, every one commits a common nuisance who does an unlawful act or fails to discharge a legal duty and thereby
(a) endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public, or-
What is the unlawful act, or what is the legal duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The unlawful act, among other things, would be the breach of the statute which the hon. member for The Battlefords read a moment ago-by discharging the effluent into the river, in contravention of a statute of the province of Alberta or regulations passed thereunder. That would be an unlawful act beyond question, if we did not go on and deal with other aspects of the crime of a common nuisance and indicate that anything which was done in contravention of the public interest might, in itself,
Criminal Code
apart from being in contravention of the statute be regarded as an unlawful act.
Is that the legal opinion of the minister's law officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a statement I am making, and for which I am taking the responsibility.

The minister always
says that he himself does not interpret the law, but that only the law officers do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am making this speech, and I am responsible for it. And if my hon. friend wishes to contradict it he will have ample opportunity to do so. But I wish he would wait until I have finished before he interrupts to contradict it.
I am not contradicting; I was just asking a question, to see what foundation there was.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Now, the proposal is to create a new offence. For reasons I have stated, I do not think that this new offence which my hon. friend is proposing to create would be satisfactory for the purpose he has in mind because, among other things, he confines the substance he wishes to prohibit to offensive volatile substances, or any chemical or synthetic chemical, or any other substance.
Now, it is true that in the present case, as would appear from the facts, chemicals were put into the river. But surely if we are going to have a section here which will serve the purposes that have been urged upon us during the present discussion, we would have to have a definition of "substance" which would be broader than merely chemicals.
It is true that my hon. friend says "or any other substance" but he precedes that by the words "volatile substance or any chemical". And I think he will agree that under the ejusdem generis rule, if you have a general term following a number of particular terms, the general term is interpreted as being of the same genus or kind as the particular terms which in the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Prince Albert refer to chemicals only. This I suggest is not a satisfactory or adequate wording.
Again my hon. friend will say that this is just captious criticism; but I assure him it is not. And it is not captious for this reason, that if my hon. friend adopts a broad enough wording to really provide a solution to this problem, and we put such broad wording into the Criminal Code, which has to have general application to the Dominion of Canada from coast to coast, then I wonder what

Criminal Code
would be the position of most of the municipalities and a large number of the industries, for example, on the Ottawa river and the St. Lawrence river system under this section which my hon. friend is proposing to move.
I do not think for one moment that my hon. friend's amendment provides a satisfactory solution to the problem of how we are to use for the purposes of the general public and the municipalities and industries of western Canada in an orderly way the waters of the South and North Saskatchewan rivers.
Make it applicable to all of Canada, because we do not want pollution anywhere else in Canada, either.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am trying to coniine my remarks to the western problem we are discussing. I think the hon. member for The Battlefords is quite right in this, that if the solution which we provide for the North and South Saskatchewan rivers were to take the form of an amendment to the Criminal Code it would be a solution which would automatically have to be applied to all the other rivers in Canada. And in judging what we should do in that regard we must keep that point in mind.
For that reason we will find that if we are to draft a law of general application for Canada we are more severely restricted in the scope we can take in, because it has to be of general application, than we would be if we were providing a solution which was tailored to the requirements of the North Saskatchewan river alone. And that is another reason why I think the amendment to the Criminal Code is not an orderly solution to this question.
I suggest this-without going into any detail

because I am not a health engineer or a chemical engineer, and I do not know what one should include in a list of substances which were to be barred by the Criminal Code from the Saskatchewan river-but I suggest that if the list were wide enough to be of value then it would be so wide that if applied now to all the rivers in Canada in existing industrial areas it would cause substantial complications which I do not think the hon. member for Prince Albert has taken into account.
For that reason it seems to me that in line with the suggestion made by the hon. member for The Battlefords there is another method of a much more orderly character which would be preferable as a method of utilizing the waters of the Saskatchewan river so that they could be used by industries, within proper limits, and by the general public in western Canada, in a manner

whereby they would both derive benefits and neither would suffer serious injury.
I think the solution is to be found in what has already been done by the international joint commission of the United States and Canada when they have addressed themselves to this subject under conditions of infinitely greater disadvantage than those which apply in connection with the Saskatchewan river. Because we are here dealing with the first signs of the problem of pollution in these western streams, whereas when the members of the international joint commission of the United States and Canada applied themselves to the question of the pollution of boundary waters between the United States and Canada, they had to come to grips with a problem that was already in an aggravated and advanced state.
How did they grapple with this problem? If my hon. friends are interested at all, they can find a reference to these points that I shall be making in the report of the international joint commission of the United States and Canada on the pollution of boundary waters published at Washington and Ottawa in 1951. I will not of course cover any large part of it for it is quite a lengthy document. But perhaps I might be permitted first of all to give an indication of what is covered in the heading of objectives of boundary waters quality control. The general objectives are these:
All wastes,-
And this will give the hon. member for Prince Albert some idea of how you would have to define effluent which you are prohibiting from the streams. I continue:
All wastes, including sanitary sewage, storm water and industrial effluents, shall be in such condition when discharged into any stream that they will not create conditions in the boundary waters which will adversely affect the use of those waters for the following purposes:	source of
domestic water supply or industrial water supply, navigation, fish and wildlife, bathing, recreation, agriculture and other riparian activities.
In general, they say, adverse conditions are caused by:
(A)	Excessive bacterial, physical or chemical contamination.
(B)	Unnatural deposits in the stream, interfering with navigation, fish and wildlife, bathing, recreation, or destructive aesthetic values.
(C)	Toxic substances and materials imparting objectionable tastes and odours to waters used for domestic or industrial purposes.
I ask the hon. member for The Battlefords to see how closely this describes some of the things that he has been complaining about. I go on:
(D)	Floating materials, including oils, grease, garbage, sewage solids, or other refuse.

Then it goes on to state in more specific terms the objectives. They say:
Specific objectives
In more specific terms, adequate controls of pollution will necessitate the following objectives for:
(A) Sanitary sewage, storm water, and wastes from water craft
Sufficient treatment for adequate removal or reduction of solids, bacteria and chemical constituents which may interfere unreasonably with the use of these waters for purposes aforementioned. Adequate protection for these waters, except in certain specific instances influenced by local conditions, should be provided if the conform M.P.M. median value does not exceed 2,400 per hundred ml. at any point in the waters following initial dilution.
Then they go on to deal with industrial wastes, first of all, under the heading:
Chemical wastes-phenolic type
I believe they are the ones that are involved in the Saskatchewan river. Then they go on to deal with chemical wastes other than phenolic. They deal with each one of these one by one, and deal specifically with the conditions in which the effluents must be at the time they are discharged into the river. Then they deal with highly toxic wastes, and with the problem that the hon. member for The Battlefords mentioned tonight, the deoxygenating of waters.
Then they provide for consultation with the various interests concerned. I am informed that far from there being any great amount of difficulty with industry in the carrying out of their objectives, they have found, certainly in several specific cases, the greatest amount of co-operation from the industries concerned. And why should there not be? The industries themselves with large investments have the strongest possible interests in seeing to it that the river upon which they, along with the other residents situate upon it, are dependent for supply of water, should be treated in an orderly and scientific manner.
I should like to read the recommendations af this report. They are not very long, and I ;hink they will shed a good deal of light upon what we might expect from an orderly approach to the problem which we have been discussing. They are as follows:
(1)	The commission recommends that the "objectives for boundary waters quality control" as set forth in this report be adopted by the two governments as the criteria to be met in maintaining boundary waters in satisfactory condition, as contemplated in that portion of Article IV of the boundary waters treaty of 1909 wherein it is stated: "It is further agreed that the waters herein defined as boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other."
(2)	The commission recommends that the remedial measures already known to be necessary as described in the accompanying reports of the
Criminal Code
technical advisers be put into effect and that additional measures be undertaken as may prove to be necessary in the future to meet the recommended "objectives".
(3)	As a procedure to insure accomplishment of the foregoing, the commission recommends that it be specifically authorized by the two governments to establish and maintain continuing supervision over boundary waters pollution through boards of control appointed by the commission. In carrying out this supervisory function, the commission shall notify those responsible for any pollution found objectionable in the light of the objectives recommended above and, in the event that assurance is not received that such pollution will be corrected in a reasonable time, shall make recommendations to the appropriate authority, having jurisdiction as to the further action deemed advisable.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that in the face of the problem which is posed by the opening of a great industrial expansion within the valleys, certainly of the North Saskatchewan river, that the only intelligent way to approach it is by this method and not by creating some new offence and haling people into police court and fining them, and when the case is closed, what then happens? Do they go and sin no more, or if they do, who is going to check them?
If they sin some more they are punished again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is the chief of police or the constable a person qualified to deal with a problem such as the one that has been mentioned, or should it not be dealt with by people who are trained in this sort of work and who know what they are talking about when they are dealing, for example, with the type of chemicals that are alleged to have caused this trouble in the North Saskatchewan river or with any other forms of river pollution?
My hon. friend might say, well, this is going to be very difficult because we will not be able to get together these western provincial governments, which, according to the arguments of both the hon. gentlemen who preceded me in this debate, apparently cannot come to an agreement in this matter. The argument is that by co-operation they cannot solve this problem, so therefore they must come down to the great white father, the federal government, and he is to force them all into position and make them agree and come to an intelligent solution of what is their common problem.
That is not the point at aU.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I say that any statement or implication of that kind is quite unwarranted; and it can be proven to be quite unwarranted in terms of what has already been done in relation to the waters of the Saskatchewan river itself. At the present time there is in

Criminal Code
existence the prairie waters control board set up by the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Canada.
What are the powers of that board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was just about to read them when my hon. friend interjected. I was a little bit hesitant about boring the committee with this long statement of powers, but since my hon. friend provokes me I have the best excuse for doing so.
You are doing a marvellous job on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friends are determined to anticipate my arguments, but I do not object to that. It shows they are at least paying attention to them.
Mr. Cold well:	Yes, I am paying close
attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does not cover pollution. It never purported to cover pollution. It was formed before the question of pollution had arisen and naturally it did not deal with something which did not exist.
The point I make, and I might put it in very brief form, is that this board has to do with what quantities of water will be let down from time to time and with the quantities which may be diverted, retained or expended in irrigation and the like.
But not the quantities polluted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Just give me a little time. I am going to come to pollution in a minute.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You have to build the Saskatchewan dam first.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suggest that just as this is the intelligent way to deal with the quantity of water which is to be in these interprovincial rivers, so the intelligent way of dealing with the quality of the water that is to be in these rivers is along the same lines. I believe the proper thing to do in this particular connection is to suggest to these prairie governments, which should be and I am confident are deeply concerned about this great problem about which the hon. member for Prince Albert has been so eloquent these many times-

I want to tell you if you
heard the people of Saskatchewan being eloquent, you would understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, and I am giving him credit. I give the people credit, too, for being eloquent. If I were in their shoes I do not know whether I would be eloquent but I would certainly be strongly articulate.
I suggest that this method of having a body of scientific men to study the problem, to ascertain what is involved in it and deal with it accordingly, offers, on the basis of the precedent of the international joint commission, by long odds the most sensible method of dealing with this problem, and infinitely more sensible than a series of police court prosecutions.
Now, let me make one or two points clear at this stage. This prairie provinces water board now is purely an advisory body. It has no overriding authority of its own at the present time. It has been set up to advise their respective governments whose representatives compose it. It is quite true that before the recommendations they make can become effective they must be ratified by the governments concerned. But I am told the board has had a good measure of success in getting their governments to adopt their recommendations. I would suggest that, as compared with any further amendments to the Criminal Code, especially if they are as inadequate as the ones suggested by the hon. member for Prince Albert, it would be infinitely preferable to have this body instructed by the governments which set it up to take over the authority to deal with the question of the quality of the water.
If, for one reason or another, they are not experts in that particular field of pollution because they are men who deal more with quantity problems than with quality problems-they should add to their numbers

people who are competent in this other field. If necessary another body of the same character could be set up.
Was it not the federal government that set it up?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it was not the great white father.

The water board in
western Canada was not set up by the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The water board in western Canada, I may inform my friend, was set up by the four governments who are parties to it.
Who are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have already named them, but I shall name them again in the same way I did a moment ago. They were the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Canada; those are the four.
This is merely a suggestion made, if you like, by an outsider from this problem. We in western Canada are just on the eve of a very large industrial expansion. This trouble we have been having is the first harbinger of a lot of other problems of the same character that will arise shortly. If we are going to deal with them in an orderly way we do not want to give this problem of the chemical or other pollution of water, which is a problem for scientists and engineers, into the hands of the chiefs of police or to throw them into the courts for solution when they can be dealt with by a body of this nature that is competent in the scientific and engineering fields.
In this respect I am completely in agreement with the hon. member for The Battle-fords. I feel this is the opportune time to take this move because in so far as these large western streams are concerned, we will be able to get in at the very beginning of the river pollution problems that are arising. From the beginning we would have that control over the problem which would have been of enormous advantage to the international joint commission if it had been able to deal earlier in their history with the problems with which it is now dealing. It is for these reasons I am very sorry that I cannot support the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before the hon. member for Prince Albert speaks I think at this stage it is my duty to remind the committee that what is under discussion is the proposed amendment by the hon. member for Prince Albert, widening the description of certain criminal offences. I am asking the
Criminal Code
committee not to allow itself to be led so far away from that amendment that we will find we are debating the merits of alternative methods of dealing with the pollution of a certain river, whereas we should be debating the applicability of the Criminal Code to that situation.
I believe members of the committee will agree with me that where I and others in the Chair have allowed a debate to get too far afield, we eventually found we were debating the merits of something that was not before the committee at all. I submit that for the guidance of the committee.

Never before in this house have I heard such a torrent of words in order to arrive at a negative position. Certainly the minister's suggestion about the water board was one of the most ludicrous I have ever heard advanced. The water board has nothing whatever to do with the quality of the water. It had to do with the allocation of water as among the three western provinces in order to determine whether or not irrigation projects should be permitted.
The minister says we are on the eve of an industrial development and, to use his own words, we ought to deal with matters such as this in an orderly way. So far as the people of Saskatchewan are concerned, those long-suffering 50,000, this will indeed be a very black Friday. A few weeks ago when the matter was under discussion the minister said he could not deal with the question then because we did not know whether there was any evidence against anyone. We did not know who the wrongdoer was, but once we found out who the wrongdoer was then we would be in a position to consider amendments to the Criminal Code.
At that time I stated that in my opinion the wrongdoer was Canadian Chemical Company. That conclusion has since been established beyond peradventure. The minister says we should follow some course similar to that of the international joint commission. That commission has done outstanding work. It has the power to act and it does act. The minister read the preamble of the powers of this body and said that in order to cover pollution in all of its various aspects there would have to be a great many terms defining the offence. But that is what the law officers were to consult about. That is the reason for the delay in connection with this matter. For almost five months now 50,000 people have been waiting for parliament to act. The province of Saskatchewan, and I hold no brief for the government of that province, cannot act. It has no

Criminal Code
power to act and the only government that can act is the government of Alberta. It is-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? We have now, as he has said, knowledge as to which company is mainly responsible for this particular pollution. But will the hon. member say whether or not in his opinion it is open to any citizen of the province of Saskatchewan or Alberta or the law officers or any private citizen in Prince Albert to take injunction proceedings against the company in these circumstances? Will the hon. member say "yes" or "no" to that question?

All I will say is that counsel who have been retained say there is no right of action, and it is counsel's opinion that is accepted. The minister has brought up the question of an injunction. But the health of the people in Saskatchewan and Manitoba has been affected by what has taken place and has been seriously undermined and the minister's department has done nothing but send out two officials-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Now, Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order-
I am speaking at the moment.
It is a point of order.
Oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Will the minister please state his point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when this debate began I refrained altogether from discussing the merits of this question, but my hon. friend has now stated that the Department of National Health and Welfare has done nothing-
Except send out two .officials.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: -and the house knows and the hon. member knows better than anyone else that department materially assisted in this matter.
That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Will the hon.
member for Prince Albert kindly allow the minister to put his point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is going to be allowed to discuss whether or not the government has done anything in this matter I want the opportunity to reply because that is not the case.
Mr. Chairman, that is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend interrupts more than anyone else in this house and when he is on the spot he can never take it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Will both hon.
gentlemen kindly resume their seats? I was about to raise the point of order which has been raised by the minister. It is my ruling that it is not within the competence of this committee at this time to discuss whether or not the Department of National Health and Welfare did or did not take certain action in connection with the Saskatchewan river. What this committee is discussing is whether or not the Criminal Code should be amended, and in that connection the situation on the Saskatchewan river certainly comes within the ambit of this discussion.
All of which indicates, Mr. Chairman, how interruptions such as those made by my hon. friend deviate and divert a discussion which comes within the ambit of your authority.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You should know.

I would like to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare speaking strictly to the subject matter of this amendment, but apparently we are not going to be able to induce him to rise from his seat to say something definite about this matter which will affect the people of Saskatchewan.
Order.
Have you another chairman over there?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, let me say that we are getting the same interference and the same jeers from the Liberal side of the house as we got a few weeks ago when we were discussing this problem. Have my hon. friends from Saskatchewan who are supporting the government said anything about this matter?
Give them a chance.
No, not one word.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. My hon. friend, perhaps for the benefit of the residents of Prince Albert, stated quite inaccurately that there were jeers on this side of the house. There was not one single jeer.

Well, Mr. Chairman, one cannot put jeers on the record and we do not broadcast these proceedings, but certainly the sounds we heard were not sounds of approval. Does the Minister of Justice say they were sounds of approval?
They were sounds of disapproval.

No, there is no answer. The people of Prince Albert and Battleford have waited five long months for action since the matter was first brought up. First it was stated that in a very short time a solution would be forthcoming. But this matter-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. My hon. friend knows very well that no one ever said what he is indicating was said and he knows that better than anyone else.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think in this case the point of order raised by the minister is very well taken. I myself did not consider that the last remarks of the hon. member for Prince Albert were directed to the Criminal Code. I suggest that the hon. member for Prince Albert bring his remarks under the standing order which states that speeches in committee must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration. If the hon. member will do that I will do my best to see that he is not interrupted.

Returning once more, without interruption, to the amendment, the Minister of Justice states that it does not cover every eventuality which might arise, that it does not cover all the facets and possibilities in connection with pollution. I therefore suggest that the minister, having available the law officers of the crown and with the experience of the international joint commission, should draft an amendment which will cover the situation. My hon. friend from The Battlefords spoke in the most restrained terms when he asked parliament to act on this question. All we ask is that in the industrial development which is commencing in western Canada no corporation in its own interests may use the rivers in western Canada or any part of Canada to the detriment of the welfare of the people as a whole. There is only one way in which that can be enforced and that is under the nuisance section. I have never heard of such a naive and pompous argument as that which the minister endeavoured to advance when he said that clause 163 dealt with religious services. That was one of the most unusual arguments-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on a point of privilege, I would just like to make a correction. What I said was that the clause in question was in that part of the code headed by the terms "disturbing religious services" and that it dealt with the throwing of stench bombs at meetings.
Criminal Code
That indicates that the minister has not read the section. I will now refer him to the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Read it.

The general heading
under which section 161 comes is "disturbing religious services". Section 162, which is part of that general section according to my hon. friend, reads as follows:
Every one who, without lawful excuse, the proof of which lies upon him, loiters or prowls at night upon the property of another person near a dwelling house situated on that property is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
What about vagrancy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No jeering there.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

Then section 163 reads as follows:
Every one other than a peace officer engaged in the discharge of his duty who has in his possession in a public place or who deposits, throws or injects or causes to be deposited, thrown or injected in, into or near any place,
(a) an offensive volatile substance ... is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Exactly. Will my hon. friend read subclause (b)? It is the crucial subclause.

We are not dealing with the stink bomb. We are dealing with volatile substances. After all, my hon. friend seems to be returning forever to the stink bomb. I am not concerned with that matter. I am concerned about the volatile substances going into the Saskatchewan river. My hon. friend says that amendment might well apply to some other section, that an offence could be created. But then after a vast explanation he says that the government does not intend to accept the amendment I suggested by way of a tentative suggestion so that at least the general purport of the demands of the people in Saskatchewan would be brought before the committee. Speaking for the government the minister has stated that no amendment will be accepted. That simply means that from now on if any corporation continues to dump substances into the Saskatchewan river, places our people's health in jeopardy, makes it impossible for people to use the water of the river that belongs to the people of Canada and is not the property of any corporation, nothing can be done.
We can do no more if he refuses that amendment. We have made our representations. We intend to bring the matter to a vote in order to find out whether or not the people in Saskatchewan are to be placed in the position that they are not to be given

Criminal Code
some assistance under the criminal law, not with respect to past offences but with respect to future offences, in order to deny the recurrence of this type of thing. We want to know what is the attitude of the government. Certainly alibis, postponements, explanations as to other statutes that might apply but do not, and references to the international joint commission have nothing whatever to do with this question. All of that may be interesting as a recital but it does not meet the problem.
The last time this matter was before the committee the minister said, "Let us just find out the facts and then we will know whether or not an amendment to the Criminal Code should be made." We now have the facts. We now know that one corporation has been pouring three thousand gallons of chemical waste into the river, and that those chemical wastes have rendered the water unusable 300, 400 and 500 miles away; and there is nothing to prevent a repetition. It was in order to punish possible repetitions of this action that this amendment was moved. It is the only way in which the health of the people can be protected under the law as it now is. Indeed, in Prince Albert we have a sanatorium. The minister himself received from Dr. Kirkby of that sanatorium a letter written on March 15 in which he set forth the facts in these words;
Hon. S. Garson,
Department of Justice,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Garson:
Please excuse handwritten letter hut have been confined to hospital here for past two months. I am superintendent of Prince Albert sanatorium, a 275-bed institution. The problem of water pollution has been a serious one for our patients. Recently a special filter was installed which was only partially successful.
This pollution question is more than a nuisance. I respectfully request that legislation be placed on our books to prohibit such flagrant disregard of the rights of others by any commercial or other organization.
Respectfully submitted,
R. W. Kirkby, M.D.
Medical Supt.
The only way in which the problem can be met is by making it a crime to do this type of thing. My hon. friend says that we should not make crimes unnecessarily, and I agree; but this is a necessary act. My hon. friend said we should proceed under section 165. Nothing of the kind. Section 165, under the heading "Nuisances", reads as follows:
Every one who commits a common nuisance and thereby
(a)	endangers the lives, safety or health of the public, or
(b)	causes physical injury to any person, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.

We cannot establish that: today. The medical doctors say it will be two years before we shall know the degree to which those who have gone ahead and used the water will be affected or not affected physically in consequence thereof.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Who said that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would he not say that the comfort of the people of Prince Albert was interfered with-
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -within the definition of public nuisance?

That is right. But again you read these words:
(a) endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public . . .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; comfort of the public.

Yes. My hon. friend has frequently referred to the ejusdem generis rule, that everything is interpreted with reference to the general words preceding it and that that is one of the reasons why counsel gave the opinion that section 165 did not constitute an offence. As I said before, and I repeat it, we cannot establish at the present time that the health is affected of individuals who are using that water; but we know that the Canadian National Railways have found that using this water in its present state is the best means by which to scale the flues of locomotives. If it does that, what must it do to human beings?

Before the vote is taken I must rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert. The river with the polluted water crosses my constituency. It is true that I have not as many people involved as have the hon. member for The Battlefords and the hon. member for Prince Albert. They both made a very good case and I do not propose to cover the ground which they have already covered. While Cumberland House is not as large as Prince Albert or Battleford, it is an older centre. The Minister of National Health and Welfare will be interested in the problems that are going to affect his department.
The loss of the supply of fish is going to present a health problem for the Indian people at Cumberland House which I think is extremely serious. I was in Prince Albert on January 22 and I want to submit that if

parliament could have adjourned for a few days to sit in Prince Albert I feel sure we would have had action before now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Before you took the chair, a point of order was raised while the hon. member for Prince Albert was speaking. The issue before the house is whether or not a particular amendment to the Criminal Code should be accepted by the government, namely an amendment to deal with the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river. I as Minister of National Health and Welfare decided that it was not desirable to intervene on a purely legal aspect of the debate but I felt that I should reserve my right if there was going to be any discussion on the merits.
The hon. gentleman now speaking is discussing the merits of our handling of this particular pollution, not the merits of the amendment. If he is going to do that I can tell him that I would want to point out that the minister of health in Saskatchewan takes violent exception to what he has just said. If the hon. gentleman is going to discuss whether or not the government of Canada has done its duty towards this particular matter, then we are going to discuss the merits of the question. But the issue before us is whether or not a particular amendment should be made and accepted. That is the issue. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact you have not had the advantage of the discussion that preceded your taking the chair, that hon. members should observe that point of order.

Before you make your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that what my hon. friend is doing is trying to point out the necessity for this amendment, and in showing that the amendment is necessary surely he has to say something about the conditions now and the effect, without the amendment, upon the people whom he represents in the house. I think my hon. friend is quite within the four corners of the discussion in showing how failure to carry this amendment will adversely affect the constituents whom he represents.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We may take it for granted that we are all aware of the seriousness of the situation.
There is no sign of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that he does not know about that. It was the Department of National Health and Welfare, in cooperation with the provinces, that was responsible for the improvement that has taken place. What the hon. member is now doing, and in another debate he would be perfectly 83276-230J
Criminal Code
in order, is seeking to establish the fact that he is interested in the problem, and because others want to keep within the rules of debate we are precluded from indicating that we are as greatly concerned as is the hon. member.
What they want is action.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: For that reason the rules of debate should be strictly observed and the merits of the pollution of the North Saskatchewan should not be discussed at this time but whether or not the proposed legal method is the one to deal with the question of pollution generally speaking, and in that regard only with this particular pollution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I feel that the point of order raised by the Minister of National Health and Welfare is well taken. On the other hand, this debate has perhaps been somewhat broader than should be allowed under the strict rules of relevancy in committee. I am not going to rule that the hon. member for Mackenzie is entirely out of order but I would ask him to co-operate with the chair in an effort to confine his remarks to the merits of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Prince Albert.

Thank you. I probably
would have been through by now if I had not been interrupted. The Minister of Justice, before you took the chair, Mr. Chairman, took about thirty minutes in indicating why he is going to oppose the amendment before us at the present time, and I think that I should be permitted to indicate that I am. going to support it and also to give reasons why I support it.
I submit that the welfare of my Indian friends, whose future is being jeopardized' because of the present situation, is a very real problem. As I said, I was in Prince Albert on the 22nd of January. The 22nd of February has passed, the 22nd of March has passed and there is still no legislation on the statute books that will give these people security for the future. If this is not the place to make some provision, then I submit that somewhere along the line the federal government should bring forward legislation that will protect the people because I think it is quite clear that people in Saskatchewan cannot take legal action that will give them the sort of protection they need.
The health of the people of Edmonton is not being affected, and I think it is ridiculous to suggest that the Indian people at Cumberland House should institute legal action against the Canadian Chemical Company, a very wealthy corporation, with a view to convincing the courts of this country that the

Criminal Code
corporation should discontinue a practice that is going to destroy food of the people of that northern area. When I was in Prince Albert on the 22nd of January I found that you could not drink tea or coffee made from the water. I would not want to take a shower or bath in this polluted water. I think hon. members do not realize what it means to have your water supply cut off so abruptly and for such a long period.
Oh, oh.

I have here the most recent issue of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix which has just come to me and it contains a story from Prince Albert to the effect that whether or not the water improved the council planned to call a conference of all those affected by the pollution to see what measures could be taken.
Oh, oh.
I am not quite sure just what I did say, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You are polluting our minds.

Anyway I am sure that I have the support of hon. members in trying to see that legislation is passed that will afford protection to the people living in these northern regions who are dependent on the water supply from the North Saskatchewan river.

I understand that the Minister of Justice has suggested that this matter is covered already by section 165 of the bill to amend the Criminal Code and that that section has already been dealt with. I would suggest that a reading of section 165 clearly indicates that it does cover this matter because it says:
(1)	Every one who commits a common nuisance and thereby
(a)	endangers the lives, safety or health of the public, or
(b)	causes physical injury to any person, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
The section goes on to define what is a common nuisance. It reads as follows:
(2)	For the purposes of this section, every one commits a common nuisance who does an unlawful act or fails to discharge a legal duty and thereby
(a) endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public . . .
I suggest that from a reading of the Alberta public health act, which was cited by the hon. member for The Battlefords, the discharge of this effluent into the river is definitely an unlawful act. My hon. friend said that there was no penalty provided but the penalty is here in the Criminal Code. If under a provincial statute it is an unlawful act

which endangers the comfort of the public it becomes a common nuisance, and section 165 says that anybody who commits a common nuisance is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for two years.
That is one ground upon which it comes within section 165. The only doubt that one could have about whether it would come under this section would arise from the fact that the common nuisance must endanger the lives, safety or health of the public. I do not think any court would have any difficulty whatever in saying that the pollution of river water, which caused people to be unwilling or unable to drink it, does endanger the health of the public where they have to rely upon that water. Certainly, as the minister pointed out, it does endanger the comfort of the public.
There is another way, I suggest, in which that comes within section 165. Some years ago the rural municipality of Cory obtained an injunction against the city of Saskatoon ordering that it should not discharge sewage into the Saskatchewan river. That injunction was a court order, and failure to obey it was an unlawful act. If they continued to disobey the injunction they would come squarely within the terms of section 165 of the act.
Surely if it is a nuisance subject to the obtaining of an injunction to discharge sewage into the river, it certainly would be possible to get an injunction to prevent the discharge of this material into the river, because it would be just as deleterious as the discharge of sewage. I have great respect for the opinion of the hon. member for Prince Albert, but I am sure he must be familiar with the fact that the rural municipality of Cory did obtain such an injunction, and that because of that the city of Saskatoon has had to make arrangements either to build a sewage disposal plant or render itself liable to be proceeded against under the Criminal Code, and the additional liability of contempt of court.
The way the law is at the present time, the actual commission of the nuisance has to be established. Once it is established it is subject to a penalty of two years. I can well understand that when this comes clearly within the "nuisance" clause of the Criminal Code, the Minister of Justice would object to having a clause like this inserted under the broad heading of "disturbing religious services", and taking it from under the heading of "nuisance", where it should be.
How would you put a company in jail for two years?

There is a provision in the Criminal Code where, when a corporation is

found guilty of an indictable offence, it can be fined rather than imprisoned. And while I do not carry in my mind the exact amount of the fine, my recollection is that it is very substantial.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I interrupt to point out that the fine is unlimited.
The minister says it is unlimited. I knew a provision of that kind was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is clause 623 in this bill.

And there is another provision that where a corporation is guilty of an offence, the officials responsible, as well as the corporation, can be proceeded against. So that I submit the amendment of the hon. member for Prince Albert would inject into the Criminal Code under the broad heading of "disturbing religious services" another matter which would introduce a measure of confusion.
Obviously this matter should be dealt with under "nuisances". I say to the minister that if there is any doubt about this being covered under the "nuisance" clause that doubt should be cleared up. However I do not think there is any doubt in my own mind that it is covered. If there is any doubt, then there should be no question about its being covered; because surely it should be a criminal offence to pollute the waters of a great river like the Saskatchewan so that the people cannot use it for drinking purposes, and so that those unfortunate people in mental hospitals or the provincial hospital at Battleford, who have no means of defending themselves, have to drink water that is practically undrinkable.
That is something that would certainly be a crime; and if there is any doubt about it, it should be made a crime. It is an interference with the health, safety and rights of the public who will use the water of a great river like the Saskatchewan river. I suggest with all deference that if it is not definitely a crime today, then parliament should make it a crime, because there can be no doubt of our competence under the constitution to declare it a crime.
However if it is fully dealt with, as the minister and the law officers of the crown are satisfied, so that action can be taken under the Criminal Code, there should be no need for an amendment. But I repeat that if there is any doubt I would strongly urge the minister to consider an amendment to section 165 to make it very clear that people do not have to go to court and get an injunction before it could be declared a crime under this section. If it is not clearly a crime
Criminal Code
or an offence under the appropriate section of the Alberta statute-as I think it is- which would bring it under section 165, then I suggest consideration should be given to making it very clear that it is an offence.
I do suggest with all deference that we make crimes many acts that are not as harmful to the public as the pollution of this great river, and the damage it has done to the people who rely upon it for drinking water. If there is any doubt about its being a crime, that doubt should be cleared up without delay or hesitation. However, as I said before, I think it is already covered.
I know the minister has given this matter careful consideration, and he appears to be satisfied that the situation is covered so that the people of Saskatchewan can take action, if this matter is not properly looked after, by bringing it into the court and having the corporation punished. If there is any doubt about their right to take that action, then without question that right should be given to them by parliament. I submit that, with all deference.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first intimation we have had from the minister or the government that there might be some legislation that would cover this pollution. But what is the position of, let us say, the city council of Prince Albert? In addition to the distress they have suffered, up to March 23 they had to spend something more than $3,000 for the hauling of water. Incidentally they hang black crepe on the doors of the houses to which the water is hauled. Then, the town of Battleford has had a well machine at a charge of $100 a day, and they have had it for some considerable time- I do not know just how long-in an effort to find water.
Apart from the distress they have suffered, will the town of Battleford, that is not in a very good financial position anyway, have to go to the expense of taking action against this company in Edmonton? Or will the federal government, under this act through which it says it has power, take action? Will it be up to the cities to take action, when they might stand the chance of losing, and thereby become liable for additional loss of money? There can be no doubt that a crime has been committed-no doubt about it- that a dastardly crime has been committed against these people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The attorney general of Saskatchewan could do it; there would be no difficulty about that.
