I have a question to ask, in an effort to get some light on the matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Comox-Alberni.

Mr. Chairman, in spite of some of the lighter exchanges that have taken place across the floor of the house I, for one, would not want to suggest that the Minister of Justice or other hon. members supporting him are not concerned about this problem. I think it is something which warrants our serious consideration. I come from the balmy slopes of the Pacific side where our water certainly will not be polluted by the North Saskatchewan. But even the hon. member who moved this amendment did indicate that he was more concerned about having something adequate done than having the amendment passed in this particular form.
The Minister of Justice made some reference to clause 165 which deals with nuisances, and possibly that may be a more appropriate place in the Criminal Code in which something could be done. But after looking at it carefully I am not convinced it is adequate to deal with the kind of situation that has been described at some considerable length; because it would seem to me, and I have been educated to a certain extent, after listening to the minister in his exposition of some of these clauses, that it is necessary under clause 165, before a matter is a nuisance which is an indictable offence, to prove that the life, safety or health of the public has been endangered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will continue reading it, he will see that it also includes their comfort.

It is not that; it is in the part which says:
For the purposes of this section, every one commits a common nuisance-
It defines what constitutes a nuisance. Is it not true that in addition to it being a nuisance it has to endanger the life, safety or health of an individual before it is an indictable offence?
Now, I cannot help but contrast the situation of having no effective action under such a section with the situation which exists in respect to the pollution of waters where fisheries are involved, and which are covered under the Fisheries Act. It would be worthwhile to contrast this clause with the section as it is set forth in the Fisheries Act, having to do with a similar offence. Section 33, subsection 2 of the Fisheries Act says:
No person shall cause or knowingly permit to pass into, or put or knowingly permit to be put, lime, chemical substances or drugs . . .
[The Chairman.]
And so on, into the water. Section 61 of the same act prescribes the penalties for committing that offence. The penalty is $20 a day for the first offence and additional penalties if the offence is persisted in of so many dollars per day. It seems to me that the way in which that type of offence is set forth and the manner in which the penalties are prescribed in the Fisheries Act clearly place the onus on the person who may put anything into the waters to establish their prior right to do so before they put anything in.
Not long ago I happened to pick up a publication in which I was interested because it described a very detailed survey of the waters of the Upper Alberni inlet and the river which runs into it, which was made several years ago at a time when it was proposed to establish a pulp mill at the head of that inlet, which would, in the course of its normal operation, discharge certain chemicals into those waters. While what the minister says with regard to the co-operation that many corporations might be willing to give may be true, at the same time we cannot help but feel the fact that what was set forth clearly in the Fisheries Act as a straightforward statement, and penalties are provided for putting chemicals into those waters, may have resulted in that particular firm being a little more cautious in building their plant and dumping the chemicals into the water, and then discovering afterwards that damage was caused.
It seems to me that in dealing with this general problem the same principle should be established in regard to the pollution of waters that are going to be used by human beings. The law should be so worded that the onus would be upon the chemical company to establish before they started constructing their plant or putting the discharges into the water that no harmful result would follow. It struck me that the illustration of what happened in the establishment of this pulp mill was in great contrast to the situation that is being discussed at the present time, where in fact the door was being locked after the horse had been stolen, or where it was necessary, after pollution had started, to go through that careful analysis by the scientists and officials described by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to establish just what was happening. In the one case all of these things were established long before the foundation of the plant was put in. In this case nothing definite was known about it until the pollution occurred miles down the river.
Perhaps there is some other body that could do something. The minister referred

to a board. I understood him to say that it was a voluntary and co-operative organization. Perhaps it could conduct the necessary scientific surveys and so on.
Nevertheless, I feel that if in the Criminal Code-if that is the place for it-or in some other act it could be clearly established that the onus is on the persons who contemplate putting chemicals or other substances in the water to show that no possible danger could arise from their action before they start to do so rather than after, and not have the onus placed upon, as the hon. member for The Battlefords said, the council of a city to take court action or seek an injunction or launch a suit for damages and pay the costs. We would thus accomplish the objective we have in mind. I am inclined to think that if clause 165 were given a proper going over with the situation that may exist in mind the principle which is set forth in the Fisheries Act could be incorporated in a clause in the Criminal Code to cover the situation.

speechtext:

the question?

Before the question is put I should like to have the minister give an opinion in regard to what I put before him. The public health act of the province of Alberta, which of course is primarily interested in the matter, sets up a provincial board to deal with this very question of watching over the supply of water from springs, wells, ponds, lakes, streams and rivers used as a public water supply in the province of Alberta. It sets up a board to supervise that sort of thing, and if there are any complaints about the pollution of any stream the provincial board is empowered to inquire into the matter and it may make a report to the minister as to what remedial measures are required in respect to the matter.
Where the provincial board recommends a remedy, then an application may be made to a judge of the supreme court by any person interested for an order to abate the nuisance. It seems to me quite clear that that is the provision made in regard to interfering with the rights of people within the province of Alberta. They have laid down how the matter should be dealt with once an order is made by the judge in regard to the matter, that this pollution of the river shall cease, based upon the fact of preserving the purity of the water supply. Then, I suggest to the minister, a person who continued to pollute the water after that would be guilty of a common nuisance. A common nuisance is described as a person who does an unlawful act, and if an injunction had been obtained from a judge that would be an unlawful act which would endanger the comfort of the public.
Criminal Code
Then it goes on to say that anyone who commits a nuisance and who does endanger the health of the public-any court would hold that interfering with the purity of the drinking water would endanger the public- would be guilty of this offence. I believe that would be one method of putting the problem clearly within the terms of section 165. Then, without getting an order from the court in Alberta, it seems to me all that would be necessary to prove a charge under section 165 would be that a common nuisance had been committed. In order to prove that it would only be necessary to prove that a person had committed an act which endangered the comfort of the public. If it was proven thereby that that was a nuisance, all that would be necessary then would be to show that it endangered the safety or health of the public.
I do not think any court would have any difficulty in finding that an act which made the waters of a river upon which thousands of people depend for their drinking water supply unfit for use for that purpose had endangered the health of the public. If the minister, who has carefully considered this matter in consultation with his officers, and I have every confidence in the law officers of the dominion government, is satisfied that this situation is covered by section 165, then I submit no amendment is necessary. On the other hand I would, of course, feel that if he is in any doubt about the matter the section should be allowed to stand so the problem can be investigated. It is not a matter about which there should be any doubt. If the minister is ready to say he is satisfied the offence is covered, then so far as I am concerned I do not see any reason for the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?
I want an answer to my question. I believe the minister can tell us whether he feels the matter is covered or is not covered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In addition to the cases which the hon. member for Rosthern has cited, Mr. Chairman, which had to do with the health board in Alberta making certain orders, I find that regulation 1007 of the regulations restricting nuisances and general sanitation in Alberta provides:
The deposit of any dead animal, manure, excreta, refuse, garbage, liquid waste or other filth upon, on. or into any street, ditch, highway, byway, wharf, dock, lake, pond, river, stream, harbour, water, well or sewer or on to any land, except with the written consent of the local board of health or the provincial board of health, shall be deemed a nuisance.

Criminal Code
I would imagine that the contravention of that would be an unlawful act within the meaning of the Criminal Code.

On clause 165-Common nuisance.

The minister suggested that perhaps clause 165 would be a better clause to amend than clause 163, Mr. Chairman. I, therefore, move that:
Subclause (2) be renumbered as (3) and that the following be inserted as subclause (2):
(2) Every one who, by himself, his agent or employee, places or discharges, or causes to be placed or discharged or suffers to be placed or discharged, in, upon or near, springs, lakes, streams or rivers, any industrial waste or any other polluting material of any kind whatsoever, which either by itself or in connection with other matter may corrupt or impair the quality of the water thereof in another province or render such water in such other province unfit for accustomed or ordinary use is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for two years, or a fine of not less than two thousand dollars.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?
No, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is still on his feet and wants to speak. It is ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again?

Agreed.
Clause stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext: On Monday, Mr. Speaker, we shall continue with this debate. When it is completed there will be a supply motion presented, and when it is carried we shall call whatever departments will be agreed upon in the meantime and then take public works.
